name: Regression fallacy
statement: Extreme measurements tend to be followed by less extreme ones for statistical reasons alone, and the fallacy is crediting that return to whatever happened in between.
meaning: Two things share the name and only one of them is about people. Regression to the mean is arithmetic. When two measurements of the same quantity correlate imperfectly, a group picked out for an extreme score on the first will, on average, sit closer to the mean on the second. Nothing pulls it back and no force is at work. The regression fallacy is the further claim that people miss this, and so hand the credit or the blame to whatever happened between the two measurements: the coaching, the pill, the reprimand, the new policy. The first half is a theorem. The second half is an empirical claim about human reasoning and has to be tested like any other, which is where the record gets thinner than the textbooks suggest.

origin.note: The bias is set out under the heading "Misconceptions of regression" in "Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases". That paper states that people do not expect regression where it is bound to occur, and that when they do notice it they invent spurious causal explanations. It credits the flight-training example to reference 1, Kahneman and Tversky's 1973 Psychological Review article. The statistical phenomenon is much older and belongs to Galton in 1886.

evidence: Galton supplied the arithmetic. His 1886 memoir worked from the heights of 930 adult children and their 205 parentages. Female statures were converted to male equivalents by a factor of 1.08, and he put the level of mediocrity in his population at 68.25 inches without shoes. His law was that the height deviate of the offspring is, on average, two-thirds of the height deviate of its mid-parentage. He explained it by ancestry rather than by imperfect correlation. The bias arrived as an anecdote. Tversky and Kahneman wrote that in a discussion of flight training, experienced instructors noted that praise for an exceptionally smooth landing is typically followed by a poorer landing on the next try. Harsh criticism after a rough landing was usually followed by an improvement. The instructors concluded that verbal rewards are detrimental to learning and verbal punishments beneficial. The paper reports no landing scores, no sample and no statistical test. Kahneman's Nobel autobiography gives the scene. He and Ozer Schild built a training course for instructors at the Air Force flight school, and one seasoned instructor answered his speech on positive reinforcement with the pattern above. Kahneman then arranged a demonstration in which each participant tossed two coins at a target behind his back. He records no measurements from it either. The nearest thing to data in the 1973 paper is its seventh problem, which asked for 95% confidence bounds on the true IQ of a person scoring 140. Its own figures, as tabulated by the 2024 replication rather than read in the original, are 108 participants, of whom 67.59% gave an interval symmetric around 140. Medicine supplies the clearest demonstration that the effect is worth guarding against. McCambridge, Kypri and McElduff followed 967 New Zealand students, of 1,480 first approached, over six months. Mean AUDIT scores rose by 0.98 points with no entry threshold, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.24. Selecting only those scoring 8 or more cut the rise to 0.43, and selecting at 20 or more turned it into a fall of 1.99 points, 95% CI minus 3.18 to minus 0.80. A trial recruiting heavy drinkers would have watched them improve without treating anybody.

replication.headline: The only registered replication located reversed the 1973 paper's regression problem: non-regressive answers fell from 68% of 108 people to 18% of 801.
replication.detail: Chan and Feldman repeated all seven problems from Kahneman and Tversky (1973) as a Registered Report, with 801 US participants recruited on Prolific, mean age 43.03. Two of the seven bear on regression and both moved away from the original. On problem 7, the interval for a true IQ behind an observed 140, the original reported 67.59% of 108 giving an interval symmetric around 140, 22.22% giving a regressive one and 10.19% a counter-regressive one. The replication found 17.60% symmetric, 76.40% regressive and 5.99% counter-regressive. Dropping intervals centred below 100 as overly regressive left 554 people at 25.45% symmetric, 65.88% regressive and 8.66% counter-regressive. The direction of the original result is gone in both readings. Self-rated statistical knowledge did not track how far people regressed, r(799) = -.032, p = .365, with a Bayes factor of 12.18 for the null on all data and 14.44 after the overly regressive answers were removed. Problem 5 asked for grade point average predictions from percentile scores on academic achievement, on a mental concentration test described as unreliable, or on sense of humour. The 1973 paper held that predictions from the unreliable measure would be no more regressive than those from achievement. In the replication the mean predicted average was 2.69 from achievement against 2.82 from mental concentration, t(521) = -3, p = .003, d = -0.26, 95% CI [-0.43, -0.09]. The within-participant spread was narrower for mental concentration, 0.73 against 0.80, t(521) = 3.1, p = .002, d = 0.27, 95% CI [0.10, 0.44]. Chan and Feldman read this as participants doubting the weak evidence and regressing their predictions accordingly, and write that people may not fail to regress when the measure of ability is disclosed as unreliable. Their overall verdict on the seven problems is mixed support; the two regression problems are the clearest departures.

study.cite: Chan, H. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Representativeness heuristic in intuitive predictions: Replication Registered Report of problems reviewed in Kahneman and Tversky (1973). Bachelor of Social Sciences thesis, University of Hong Kong, deposited at OSF project 8zhcj.

limits: The replication tested one thing the fallacy is said to cover, non-regressive numerical prediction, and not the causal misattribution that gives the fallacy its name. Two studies that did test that could not be read. Schaffner's "Specious learning about reward and punishment" is closed at the publisher. Hogarth and Soyer's four experiments in Decision are recorded by Unpaywall as closed with no repository copy. Neither abstract could be obtained from Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall or the publisher, so nothing either found is stated here. The one direct test whose result was read is a preprint. Harris, Schulte and Alves report four preregistered experiments, total N = 601. Participants asked to recover true probabilities from other people's estimates shifted those estimates towards the mean rather than away from it, reinforcing the regressiveness instead of correcting it. That is about reading other people's judgements, not about a treatment applied between two measurements, and it has not been peer reviewed. The 1973 paper itself could not be opened, so every figure attributed to it above is read off the replication's table of the target article's reported statistics. The replication's own Study 5 table reports condition sizes of 436, 437 and 436 for a study of 801 participants, which does not reconcile with its between-subjects description, and the discrepancy was not resolved. Statisticians warning about regression are not immune to it. Barnett, van der Pols and Dobson's 2005 guide to computing the expected regression effect carried a wrong formula for ten years. Their 2015 correction restates the worked example's correlation as 0.36 rather than 0.64, raising the expected effect from 9.6 mg/dl to 17.3. No peer-reviewed test of the Sports Illustrated cover jinx was found. A Crossref search on the phrase returns one relevant record, a 2011 PsycEXTRA item by Reifman and Cohadarevic titled "The Sports Illustrated jinx in golf: A control-group study". It is registered as a dataset and carries no abstract in that record. Web searches surfaced only blogs, encyclopedia articles and news items. The 2,456 covers and 37.2% rate that circulate everywhere come from the magazine's own 2002 cover story, which could not be obtained.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat regression as a force. It is a property of selection under imperfect correlation, and the individual measurement is not owed a correction. That distinguishes it from the gambler's fallacy, where the next outcome is imagined to compensate for the last: regression says the group average moves, not that any particular case is due for a reversal. The second error runs the other way. Showing that regression can explain an apparent improvement does not show that the treatment did nothing, only that the before-and-after comparison cannot tell. A randomised control group settles what a pre-post difference cannot. The third concerns the flight instructors. What Tversky and Kahneman published is a report of what instructors said about landings, not a measurement of landings, and the entry above found no analysis of instructor feedback against landing scores in the searches described. The story is evidence of how the idea was arrived at, and it circulates as though it were the study that established it. Kahneman's own account differs from the retellings in one detail worth keeping straight. The demonstration he ran used two coins tossed at a target behind the back, and he reports its result as something the room could see rather than as recorded data.

sources.text: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131. Read in full from a scan of the JSTOR copy; the source for the wording of the flight-training passage and for the two claims about how people handle regression.

Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1973). On the psychology of prediction. Psychological Review, 80(4), 237-251. Closed on every route tried, including PsycNet, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall. Its bibliographic record was verified at Crossref. No figure attributed to it here was read in it.

Galton, F. (1886). Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature. The Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, 15, 246-263. Read in full as the scan at galton.org; the source for the 930 children, the 205 parentages, the 1.08 factor, the 68.25 inches and the two-thirds law.

Kahneman, D. (2003). Autobiography. In T. Frangsmyr (Ed.), Les Prix Nobel 2002. Read in full at nobelprize.org; the source for the flight-school course, the instructor's reply and the coin-tossing demonstration.

Chan, H. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Representativeness heuristic in intuitive predictions: Replication Registered Report of problems reviewed in Kahneman and Tversky (1973). University of Hong Kong thesis, deposited at OSF. Read in full as the deposited PDF; the source for every replication figure above and for the original's problem 5 and problem 7 counts.

Rahal, R.-M. (2024). The Representativeness Heuristic Revisited: Registered Replication Report of Kahneman and Tversky (1973). Peer Community in Registered Reports, 31 May 2024. The recommendation record for the replication above. Only its Crossref record was checked; the article page returned an access-denied response.

Harris, C., Schulte, A., & Alves, H. (2025). Regressive Judgments: How People Fail to Account for Regression in Other People's Judgments. Preprint posted 7 August 2025. Abstract read through the OSF API; the four experiments and the total N = 601 come from it. Not peer reviewed.

McCambridge, J., Kypri, K., & McElduff, P. (2014). Regression to the mean and alcohol consumption: A cohort study exploring implications for the interpretation of change in control groups in brief intervention trials. Drug and Alcohol Dependence, 135, 156-159. Read in full at PubMed Central; the source for the 967 participants and every AUDIT figure above.

Barnett, A. G., van der Pols, J. C., & Dobson, A. J. (2005). Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it. International Journal of Epidemiology, 34(1), 215-220. Abstract read; the full text is behind Oxford's paywall and no claim above rests on its body.

Barnett, A. G., van der Pols, J. C., & Dobson, A. J. (2015). Correction to: Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it. International Journal of Epidemiology, 44(5), 1748. The correction's wording, the 0.36 correlation and the move from 9.6 to 17.3 mg/dl were read twice, on two separate Oxford URLs for the notice.

Schaffner, P. E. (1985). Specious learning about reward and punishment. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 48(6), 1377-1386. Named because it is the experimental test of the reward-and-punishment claim; closed at the publisher and not read, so nothing it found is reported above.

Hogarth, R. M., & Soyer, E. (2021). Regression to the mean: Experimental evidence and a proposed heuristic. Decision, 8(3), 133-154. Four experiments on how people handle regression. Recorded by Unpaywall as closed with no repository copy; the abstract could not be obtained, so nothing it found is reported above.

Reifman, A., & Cohadarevic, D. (2011). The Sports Illustrated jinx in golf: A control-group study. PsycEXTRA. The one relevant record a Crossref search on the cover jinx returns; registered as a dataset, carrying no abstract in that record, and not read.
